f.p: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC), Panama
f.t: Bribri communities also live in Panama, where the 2023 census counted 766 Bribri people.
In 1978 the University of Costa Rica published Biyöchőkname, a cultural periodical in the Bribri language; its issues are now free to read online.
The Bribri language is spoken on both sides of Costa Rica's Talamanca mountains, in Limón and Puntarenas, in three regional varieties named for Amubre, Coroma and Salitre.

n.l: The Talamanca mountains of southern Costa Rica, on both the Caribbean (Limón) and Pacific (Puntarenas) sides, with smaller communities in Bocas del Toro, Panama

f.p: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC), Panama
f.t: Panama's 2023 census counted 23,898 Buglé people; about 12,000 of them live in the Ngäbe-Buglé comarca, which they share with the Ngäbe.

f.p: FAOLEX, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
f.t: Under Panama's 1997 comarca law, the comarca's General Congress is the highest body for the ethnic and cultural voice and decisions of the Ngäbe-Buglé people.

n.l: The Ngäbe-Buglé comarca and nearby areas of Bocas del Toro and Veraguas in western Panama

f.t: Costa Rica's 2013 list of Indigenous territories includes Cabécar territories such as Alto Chirripó, Bajo Chirripó, Talamanca Cabécar, Ujarrás and Telire.
Costa Rica's 2011 census found that 87.6 percent of people in the official Cabécar territories speak the Cabécar language.

n.l: Indigenous territories in the Talamanca mountains and Chirripó area of Costa Rica, in Limón, Cartago and Puntarenas provinces

f.t: Ch'orti' is also spoken in Honduran communities such as Cabañas, Santa Rita and Copán Ruinas.
In 2025 the Academy of Mayan Languages of Guatemala translated the national symbols into Ch'orti'; the flag, for example, is tz'apray b'ujk.

f.p: Academia de Lenguas Mayas de Guatemala (ALMG)
f.t: The Ch'orti' linguistic community spans Jocotán, Camotán, Olopa and Quezaltepeque in Chiquimula and La Unión in Zacapa, Guatemala.

n.l: Jocotán, Camotán, Olopa and Quezaltepeque in Chiquimula and La Unión in Zacapa, Guatemala, and communities around Copán in Honduras

f.p: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC), Panama
f.t: Panama's 2023 census counted 51,657 Emberá people.

f.p: FAOLEX, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
f.t: Panama's Law 22 of 1983 created the Emberá comarca in Darién and named its General Congress the highest traditional decision-making body of the Emberá people.

f.p: UNICEF Latin America and the Caribbean
f.t: Bilingual storybooks in Emberá and Spanish are among the learning materials made for the early education of Emberá children in Panama.

n.l: The Emberá-Wounaan comarca and collective lands in Darién and eastern Panama, and the Pacific and Chocó regions of Colombia

f.t: In 2024, Belize observed Garifuna Settlement Day on 19 November as one of its official public holidays.
UNESCO first honored Garifuna language, dance and music in 2001 and inscribed them on its Representative List of humanity's living heritage in 2008.
Most Garifuna communities today are in Honduras, Guatemala, Nicaragua and Belize, and the Garifuna language is part of the Arawakan family.

n.l: Caribbean coast of Honduras, Belize, Guatemala and Nicaragua, plus large diaspora communities

f.t: Gunayala's 49 communities govern themselves together through the Guna General Congress, their highest political and administrative body for land, resources and education.
Gunayala runs along Panama's Caribbean coast to the Colombian border, with about 315 km of coastline and over 400 small islands and islets.
Guna authors note that their self-government existed long before any state law recognized it; Panama's Law 16 of 1953 legally organized the comarca now called Gunayala.

n.l: Gunayala on Panama's Caribbean coast and islands, plus Madungandí and Wargandí in Panama and communities in northwestern Colombia

f.t: Ixil women weavers of the Q'imb'al initiative, with youth and village ancestral authorities, launched Community Radio Tiichajil Tenam in Nebaj to share Ixil cultural values.
In 2020 Guatemala's Constitutional Court ruled in favor of the Maya Ixil people of Nebaj, restoring their ownership of the communal land of Ak'ul.

n.l: The Ixil region of northern Quiché, Guatemala: Nebaj, Chajul and Cotzal

f.p: Vereniging van Inheemse Dorpshoofden in Suriname (VIDS)
f.t: Suriname's Indigenous village leaders say legal recognition of collective rights is an obligation, not a policy choice, and in 2026 urged full implementation of the Kaliña and Lokono judgment.

f.p: Vereniging van Inheemse Dorpshoofden in Suriname (VIDS)
f.t: In Suriname the Kari'na (Kaliña) live in many villages with their own village heads, including Christiaankondre and Langamankondre at Galibi in Marowijne district.

n.l: Coastal Suriname and French Guiana, with related communities in Guyana, Venezuela and Brazil

f.t: In July 2024, voters in the Kalinago Territory elected their Kalinago Chief; the winning candidate received about 58 percent of the votes counted.

f.p: Division of Culture, Government of the Commonwealth of Dominica
f.t: Kalinago Barana Autê, a heritage site inside the territory, shares Kalinago ways of life with visitors through traditional buildings, craft making and cultural performance.

f.p: Division of Culture, Government of the Commonwealth of Dominica
f.t: The Kalinago Territory has its own local government: a Chief and six councillors elected by residents every five years, alongside representation in Dominica's parliament.

n.l: The Kalinago Territory on the northeast coast of Dominica, in the eastern Caribbean

f.t: In 2022 the United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples was a member of the Maya Kaqchikel people.
In 2021 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled in favor of the Maya Kaqchikel of Sumpango and other communities, upholding Indigenous rights to free expression through community radio.
Community Radio Naköj in Santo Domingo Xenacoj, working since 2013, produces programs in Kaqchikel and Spanish for about 7,000 Kaqchikel listeners.

n.l: Central highlands of Guatemala, including Chimaltenango, Sacatepéquez and parts of Sololá

f.t: In Totonicapán, the 48 Cantones is a K'iche' ancestral authority built from community governments, with representatives chosen each year in assembly.
The 48 Cantones' system of caring for forests and water has served as an example for communities all over Guatemala.

n.l: Western highlands of Guatemala, including Quiché, Totonicapán, Quetzaltenango and Sololá

f.t: COPINH runs Lenca community radio stations that share news bulletins, podcasts, interviews and training with Lenca communities.
COPINH, a community-based organization of the Lenca people that has worked for 30 years, is present in five departments of Honduras.
A community journalism program trained 24 Lenca women and 17 men as community correspondents, starting during the COVID-19 pandemic.

n.l: Western and southwestern Honduras (Intibucá, Lempira, La Paz and nearby departments) and eastern El Salvador

f.p: Vereniging van Inheemse Dorpshoofden in Suriname (VIDS)
f.t: In August 2026, Suriname's Indigenous village leaders asked the government to fully carry out the Kaliña and Lokono land rights judgment and protect ancestral lands in law.

f.p: Language Documentation & Conservation, University of Hawai'i Press
f.t: Lokono village representatives founded Wadian Bokotothi, meaning 'Language Keepers', and helped share one common Lokono spelling across Suriname, French Guiana and Guyana.

f.p: Vereniging van Inheemse Dorpshoofden in Suriname (VIDS)
f.t: Suriname's association of Indigenous village leaders lists the Lokono among the country's four major Indigenous peoples, with villages such as Washabo, Apoera and Alfonsdorp.

n.l: Coastal and river villages of Suriname, Guyana and French Guiana

f.t: In October 2025, the Mam communities of Cajolá and Todos Santos Cuchumatán joined two other Maya communities in reporting to a UN committee on their community radio rights.
B'alam Stereo in Cabricán, among the longer-running Indigenous stations in Guatemala's highlands, has served the Maya Mam since 1976, with work promoting education, health, water and justice.

f.p: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México
f.t: Mam crafts vary by community and include baskets, pottery, wool mantillones, palm hats, wooden toys and decorated gourds.

f.p: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México
f.t: An 1882 border treaty between Mexico and Guatemala left the Mam people divided between the two countries.

n.l: Western highlands of Guatemala (Huehuetenango, San Marcos, Quetzaltenango) and neighboring Chiapas, Mexico

f.t: Nicaragua's Bosawás Biosphere Reserve, in the Mosquitia region, is ancestral territory of the Mayangna and Miskitu peoples, whose rights there are recognized.
After the 2020 hurricanes, Mayangna communities in Bonanza rebuilt together: they repaired 15 roofs collectively and planted 50 plots of grains, beans, corn and cassava.

n.l: The Bosawás region and North Caribbean Coast of Nicaragua, with related Tawahka communities in Honduras

f.t: In 2021 the Yapti Tasba community radio network, linked to Miskitu organization YATAMA, reached 17 Indigenous territories and 154 communities, 95 percent of them Miskitu.
In 2013 Honduras titled over 1.6 million acres of coastal land in La Moskitia to the Miskitu, in seven land areas that include 128 communities.
Nicaragua's Caribbean Coast autonomy law affirms that Indigenous communities there have the right to keep and develop their languages and to bilingual education.

n.l: The Caribbean coast of Nicaragua and La Moskitia in northeastern Honduras, along the Wangki (Coco) River

f.t: In 2022 a Free, Prior and Informed Consultation Protocol for the Maya of southern Belize was adopted, and in 2025 a working draft on protecting Maya customary land tenure followed.
A 2015 Caribbean Court of Justice judgment obliges Belize's government to mark out and register Maya village lands in the south and guard them against outsiders.

n.l: The Toledo District of southern Belize and nearby Petén, Guatemala

f.t: In Santo Domingo de Guzmán, Nahuat-speaking teachers created Nahuatl cribs where children learn the language, and Radio Sensunat promotes Nahuat Pipil culture.
Izalco is the only municipality in El Salvador with an ancestral Indigenous government, made up of mayordomos and mayordomas.
In 2014 El Salvador amended article 63 of its constitution to recognize Indigenous Peoples and commit to policies supporting their identity and culture.

n.l: Western El Salvador, especially Sonsonate and Ahuachapán departments

f.p: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC), Panama
f.t: Panama's 2023 census counted 5,568 people who identify as Naso.
The Naso are led by a king who lives in Sieyik, where Panama's president came in 2020 to sign the law creating their comarca.
In December 2020 Panama created the 1,600 square kilometer Naso Tjër Di comarca, the result of decades of Naso efforts to secure their land rights.

n.l: The Naso Tjër Di comarca along the Teribe River in Bocas del Toro, northwestern Panama, near the Costa Rican border

f.p: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC), Panama
f.t: Panama's 2023 census counted 444,878 Ngäbe people.

f.p: FAOLEX, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
f.t: Panama's Law 10 of 1997 created the Ngäbe-Buglé comarca and made its lands the collective property of the comarca, closed to private sale.

n.l: The Ngäbe-Buglé comarca in western Panama (parts of Bocas del Toro, Chiriquí and Veraguas), nearby lands in Panama, and Ngäbe territories in southern Costa Rica

f.t: Radio Chiquixji in Alta Verapaz, Guatemala, broadcasts for bilingual Q'eqchi' and Spanish speakers and for communities that speak only Q'eqchi'.
In southern Belize, 39 Q'eqchi' and Mopan Maya communities have rights to their customary lands, as Belize's highest appeals court affirmed in 2015.

n.l: Alta Verapaz, Izabal and Petén in Guatemala, and the Toledo District of southern Belize

f.t: Radio Sembrador, a community station in San Pedro La Laguna on Lake Atitlán, broadcasts news and cultural programs in Tz'utujil and Spanish.
In Santiago Atitlán, a Tz'utujil traditional authority welcomed Indigenous youth from three countries in 2013 and spoke in Tz'utujil about the role of ancestral authorities.

n.l: The southern shore of Lake Atitlán in Sololá, Guatemala, including Santiago Atitlán and San Pedro La Laguna

f.p: DANE (National Administrative Department of Statistics, Colombia)
f.t: Colombia's 2018 census counted 380,460 people who identify as Wayuu, up 40.7 percent from 2005.
Wayuu justice rests on dialogue: respected mediators called Pütchipü'üi, or palabreros, settle disputes between clans through repair and compensation. UNESCO listed this system in 2010.
The Wayuu live on the Guajira Peninsula, which spans the border between Colombia and Venezuela.

n.l: The Guajira Peninsula, shared by northern Colombia (La Guajira) and northwestern Venezuela (Zulia)

f.p: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC), Panama
f.t: Panama's 2023 census counted 10,634 Wounaan people.

f.p: Yale Environment 360, Yale School of the Environment
f.t: Wounaan forest technicians map illegal clearing with smartphone apps and GIS, and communities bring that evidence to the Wounaan National Congress.

n.l: Darién and eastern Panama, including the Emberá-Wounaan comarca and collective lands, and the San Juan River region of Colombia

f.t: In May 2024 the Parliament of the Xinka People hosted Guatemala's president in San Juan de Arana, Cuilapa, where they signed a 13-point work agenda.

f.p: Universidad de San Carlos de Guatemala, Dirección General de Investigación
f.t: In Santa Rosa, the Xinka People's Council (COPXIG), a local cooperative and the departmental education office work together to restore and teach the Xinka language.

f.p: Universidad de San Carlos de Guatemala, Dirección General de Investigación
f.t: Communal lands, and the community organizations that manage them, remain a core part of Xinka identity in Jalapa, Jutiapa and Santa Rosa.

n.l: Santa Rosa, Jutiapa and Jalapa departments in southeastern Guatemala
